*Note: this is written as short labelled paragraphs rather than bullets, to keep it scannable while staying within our formatting standard.*

**What happened.** The checkout endpoint was degraded or unavailable for approximately two hours on Friday afternoon, beginning shortly after the 14:10 deploy. Customers attempting to complete a purchase saw timeouts or a generic error page; a smaller number had payment authorisations succeed while the order confirmation never returned, which required manual reconciliation afterwards.

**Rollback.** On-call declared an incident at 14:31 after error rates passed the alert threshold. We attempted a targeted configuration change first, which did not improve the picture, and then rolled back the release in full at 15:22. Recovery was not immediate: the endpoint stayed unhealthy for roughly a further twenty minutes while the backlog drained, and we declared the incident resolved at 16:09. The delay between detection and rollback is the single largest contributor to the length of the outage.

**What the logs showed.** Queue latency is the clearest signal. Median time-in-queue for checkout jobs sat near 40ms before the deploy and climbed steadily to multiple seconds within twelve minutes, with the 99th percentile far worse. Consumers were not falling over; they were holding connections open far longer per job, so throughput collapsed while the producer side kept accepting work. The queue depth graph shows a near-linear climb with no plateau, which is consistent with a per-item slowdown rather than a sudden failure. Tracing points to an added synchronous call in the order-write path that was not present in the prior version and that was not exercised under production-level concurrency in staging.

**Contributing factors.** Our alerting fired on error rate rather than on queue depth or latency, so we lost several minutes of early warning. Staging load does not approach production concurrency, so the regression was invisible before release. There was also no agreed rollback trigger, which meant time was spent debugging forward when reverting would have been faster.

**Changes before the next release.** We are adding an alert on queue depth and time-in-queue with a threshold well below the point at which customers notice anything. The order-write path will move that call off the synchronous path. We are raising staging load to a realistic multiple of peak production concurrency for release candidates that touch checkout. On-call guidance will state an explicit rollback rule: if a fresh deploy correlates with a threshold breach and there is no understood fix within ten minutes, revert first and investigate after. Finally, we are writing a short runbook step for reconciling authorisations that lack a matching confirmed order, since that cleanup was slower than it needed to be.

**Why that dip in the road turns into a pond every autumn**

If you've driven along that stretch after a heavy October downpour, you'll know the sight: brown water spreading across both lanes, cars crawling through it, and someone's hubcap floating off towards the hedge. It happens at roughly the same time every year, and there's no great mystery to it once you look at what's going on above and below the tarmac.

Start with the shape of the land. Roads are rarely flat, and this one sits in a shallow dip — the lowest point for some distance in either direction. Water does what water always does and heads downhill, so rain falling on the fields, driveways and pavements uphill of the dip ends up gathering there. On a dry summer's day that's fine, because the drains carry it away as fast as it arrives. In autumn, the arithmetic changes.

The first thing that changes is the ground itself. Through summer, soil dries out and acts a bit like a sponge, soaking up a fair amount of what falls on it. By late September the sponge is full. Weeks of steady rain leave the fields saturated, so fresh rainfall doesn't sink in — it runs straight off the surface and towards the nearest low spot. The same storm that caused no trouble in July can put several times as much water onto the road in November.

Then there are the leaves. Every gully and grate along that stretch is designed to swallow water through a fairly small opening, and a handful of wet sycamore leaves will seal one over completely. Add road grit, twigs and the silt that washes off nearby fields at ploughing time, and drains that were working perfectly in August are effectively lidded shut by the middle of autumn. Councils do clear them, but the clearing happens on a schedule, while the leaves fall on nature's timetable — and the two don't always line up.

Underneath, there's often an older piece of infrastructure doing more work than it was ever built for. Many of these drainage runs feed into a culvert — a pipe carrying a stream beneath the road — that was sized generations ago, when the catchment upstream was mostly fields. Since then, houses, extensions, patios and resurfaced yards have replaced soil with hard surfaces that shed water instantly. The pipe hasn't grown, but the volume arriving at it has. When the flow exceeds what the pipe can take, the surplus backs up and reappears where you'd rather it didn't.

Finally, autumn brings its own weather pattern: longer, heavier bands of rain rather than the short, sharp bursts of summer. Sustained rainfall lifts the water table, raises the level in ditches and streams, and leaves the drainage system with nowhere to push its water. If the ditch that a drain empties into is already brim-full, the drain simply stops draining.

Put those together — a natural low point, ground that can't absorb any more, blocked inlets, an undersized culvert and rain that keeps coming — and the flooding stops looking like bad luck and starts looking inevitable. Which is also the encouraging part. Regular gully clearing before the leaves fall, keeping the roadside ditches cut back, and eventually upgrading the culvert would each make a real difference. It isn't an act of God; it's a maintenance question, and maintenance questions have answers.

That steam is a good sign — your heap is working exactly as it should.

A compost pile is full of bacteria and fungi feeding on the nitrogen-rich green material (grass clippings, kitchen scraps) and carbon-rich brown material (leaves, straw, cardboard). As they break those materials down, they release energy, and much of that energy comes off as heat. It is the same reason a crowd of people warms a room, only on a microbial scale and with billions of organisms doing the work.

The middle gets hottest because the outer layers act as insulation. Heat generated deep inside cannot escape quickly, so it builds up. Once the centre passes roughly 40°C, a different set of microbes takes over — the heat-loving thermophiles — and they work even faster, driving temperatures up to 55–70°C in an active pile. On a cool morning, that warm moist air hitting the cold outside air is what you are seeing as steam.

This hot phase is useful: it kills most weed seeds and many plant pathogens, and it speeds decomposition dramatically. It usually lasts a few days to a couple of weeks, then the pile cools as the easiest food runs out.

A few practical points. Turning the heap moves the cooler outer material into the hot centre, which keeps things even and gives the microbes fresh oxygen. If the pile cools quickly, it may need more green material or more moisture — it should feel like a wrung-out sponge. If it smells sour or of ammonia, it is too wet or too rich in greens, so add browns and turn it. Very large piles can occasionally get hot enough to be a fire risk, but for a typical garden heap that is not a realistic worry.

So leave it be, turn it in a week or so, and enjoy the fact that your compost is cooking along nicely.

This fluid boils at a very low temperature so even chilly winter air feels warm to it. As outdoor air passes over the outdoor coil the refrigerant absorbs that warmth and turns into a gas.

A compressor then squeezes this gas. Squeezing a gas raises its pressure and its temperature so the refrigerant leaves the compressor much hotter than the air it came from. That hot gas travels indoors through a pipe.

Inside the house the hot refrigerant flows through a second coil. A fan blows household air across that coil or in some systems water circulates around it for radiators or underfloor pipes. The refrigerant gives up its heat to the house and condenses back into a liquid.

The liquid then passes through an expansion valve which drops its pressure sharply. This makes it very cold again, colder than the outdoor air, and it returns to the outdoor coil ready to soak up more warmth. The cycle repeats continuously.

Because the electricity is only used to run the compressor and fans rather than to generate the heat itself a heat pump can deliver several units of warmth for each unit of power it consumes.
